subject: adult-health-surgery
title: Shoulder, arm and hand injuries: key emergency patterns

steps.tx: Shoulder, arm and hand injuries are common in trauma and sports. Start with the **neurovascular check**, because it decides urgency. Test the radial or ulnar pulse, capillary refill, and sensation over the key nerve areas before and after any reduction or splint. A deficit recorded before treatment gives a clear baseline for later review.

steps.tx: Anterior shoulder dislocation can injure the **axillary nerve**, which supplies deltoid and skin over the regimental badge area. Numbness there after dislocation suggests nerve injury. Most cases are neurapraxias that recover over weeks to months. A normal radial pulse shows the arterial supply is intact, so this is a nerve problem rather than a vascular emergency.
steps.say: Anterior shoulder dislocation can injure the axillary nerve, which supplies deltoid and skin over the regimental badge area. Numbness there after dislocation suggests nerve injury. steps.tx: A deep hand infection can track along the tendon. A **flexor sheath infection** shows a flexed finger, fusiform swelling and pain on passive extension. Fever and a raised white count and CRP indicate spread. The closed sheath traps pus, which compresses tendon blood supply. Urgent surgical drainage with intravenous antibiotics is needed to prevent tendon necrosis.

steps.tx: A fall on the outstretched hand with **snuffbox tenderness** points to scaphoid fracture, even when early wrist X-rays look normal. Pain on longitudinal thumb compression supports the diagnosis. Immobilise in a thumb spica splint and repeat imaging after about two weeks, or use MRI or CT when available. Early immobilisation reduces the risk of nonunion.

steps.tx: Crush injury with dark urine, very high **creatine kinase** and hyperkalaemia suggests rhabdomyolysis. Muscle necrosis releases myoglobin, which injures renal tubules and causes acute kidney injury. Treatment is early intravenous fluids and close potassium monitoring. Tense swelling after a crush or fracture also needs compartment assessment, since the two problems often coexist.

steps.tx: **Compartment syndrome** is a surgical emergency. Warning signs are pain out of proportion, pain on passive finger stretch, a tense compartment and rising analgesic need. A present pulse does not exclude it. Rising pressure reduces perfusion until muscle and nerve damage becomes irreversible. Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment, not elevation or repeated observation.

steps.tx: A **mallet finger** follows a fingertip blow that tears the extensor tendon from the distal phalanx. The distal joint droops and cannot be extended. If there is no subluxation, treat with a continuous splint holding the distal joint straight for about six to eight weeks. Active flexion of the fingertip must be avoided, because it separates the repair.
